subject: Correcting abundance for seabirds in directional flight biased towards the line

messages.author: 62cc45150b4a6799
messages.subject: Correcting abundance for seabirds in directional flight biased towards the line
parts:
Hello my name is Jeff.  
I'm new to distance sampling but grateful to have found this resource. 


I am working with an older shipboard seabird survey dataset where behavior was recorded. The radial distances were recorded in bins out to 300 m. I noticed that the data is zero-inflated and upon further investigation the high number of counts on the line are primarily driven by birds that were assigned the behavior "directional flight" (15% of birds in this behavior category have a perpendicular distance of zero). Binning the data does not alleviate the zero-inflation.

I suspect that in-flight birds were observed approaching the line from the non-survey side of the ship and recorded as they passed the line and through the survey area, causing an increase in zeros - The majority of radial distances are in the 200-300m and the majority of angles are zero. When I constrain the analysis to only include birds with the behavior of "sitting", "foraging", and "circling" the detection function is far more reasonable. But now of course I'm ignoring the birds in directional flight. For the purposes of relative abundance across the area this isn't such a bad thing but I'd like to correct for birds in directional flight if possible. 

I came across a passage in the Buckland et al. 2015 (sec 10.2.1) 

"Another solution to birds in flight is to survey only birds on the sea, then separately estimate the proportion of time spent flying, so that the abundance estimate can be adjusted for flying birds." This is a good solution but I'm afraid I don't have the accompanying data to inform this. 

Has anyone experienced this issue before - or have any ideas about incorporating these directional flight birds into abundance estimates? Or perhaps treating the bird in directional flight as a totally separate analysis?

Sincerely grateful for your time and thoughts,

Jeff

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Correcting abundance for seabirds in directional flight biased towards the line
parts:
Jeff

Welcome to the email list.  You indeed are working with a data set that contains some tricky bits.  Animal movement poses challenges in performing abundance estimation from distance sampling.

You also note that the survey employed one-sided transects.  This protocol is briefly mentioned in Buckland et al. (2015, Sect 10.5.2) and is something that should be avoided, because as you note, animals that appear from the "off effort" side of the ship contribute considerably to the spike in detections at distance zero, consequently resulting in a detection function that drops off rapidly, producing positive bias in the abundance estimates.

I don't have any magic solutions to this set of circumstances. Here are a couple of untested suggestions (don't think there is support in the literature for them).

  • If the bird flight is directional, is the flight direction recorded in the data?  If so, perhaps you could exclude birds flying from the off-effort direction.
  • Another situation where "spike at zero" data arises is in jungle situations where transects are cut into vegetation, resulting in detections at distance in the forward direction, but poor detection in other directions.  One possible approach in both the jungle situation as well as your situation is to invoke a "forward truncation" criterion.  Admittedly, the decision regarding that forward distance will be subjective, and open to dispute.  But given you have distance and bearing, you have the opportunity to exclude flying birds that are at distance and at small angles.

Just to round out the discussion, I presume you are aware of the 1984 paper by Tasker et al. that describes methodology dealing with shipboard seabird surveys:

Tasker, Mark L., Peter Hope Jones, Tim Dixon, and Barry F. Blake. 1984. Counting Seabirds at Sea from Ships: A Review of Methods Employed and a Suggestion for a Standardized Approach. The Auk 101 (3): 567–77. https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/101.3.567.

messages.author: b8a1da45c9a2eab1
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Correcting abundance for seabirds in directional flight biased towards the line
parts:
Hi Jeff,

Further to Eric's final comment, are you aware that seabirds at sea surveys often employ rather different methods to survey birds first detected on the water and those first detected in flight? Birds on the water generally move slowly with respect to the survey vessel, so they can readily be analysed in a distance sampling framework. In contrast, birds in flight, generally move faster than the vessel, violating one of the assumptions of distance sampling. In short, the motion of birds relative the survey vessel results in an increase in encounter rate. Tasker et al. proposed a 'snapshot' method to deal with this (but see Gaston, Auk, 104(2): 336-338 fro limitations). In effect, this is a plot survey for birds in flight, carried out simultaneously with the distance sampling survey for birds on the water. It's called the snapshot method because birds in flight are recorded instantaneously at a regular interval. In some methods, the interval is such that birds are recorded in a 300 m x 300 m box every 300 m along the track line. You may find that your surveyors used something similar, or that your data can be thinned in a way that mimics this technique.

By the way, I note that your data set includes distances to birds detected in flight. It would be worth checking how these distances were estimated (using some sort of rangefinder or by eye?) because measuring distances to flying seabirds is notoriously difficult. Some analyses simply assume that birds in flight are detected perfectly within the 300 x 300 m snapshot box described above. This seems reasonable for large, conspicuous species. With this in mind, Dave Miller has been developing some extensions to the dsm() function that allow data with two detection functions (i.e. detection varies with distance for birds on the water and detection is perfect for birds in flight) to be treated in the same model. It might be worth contacting him if you're interested in density surface modelling with your data. If you're just looking for a design-based abundance estimate, I would suggest treating your on-water and in-flight separately, using a distance sampling analysis for the former and plot sampling analysis for the latter.

All the best,

Ewan

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Correcting abundance for seabirds in directional flight biased towards the line
parts:
These are fantastic recommendations. 
After looking into each of these thoughts and considering the limits of the dataset -  I think that I will further explore the possibilities of  "front truncating" and treating on-water birds and in-flight birds separately. Removing some of the far off in-flight birds (maybe >200 m) and using a plot sampling analysis in addition to a distance sampling analysis for the on-water birds seems reasonable and will at least give me the capacity to compare relative densities across the project area. 

I will also be excited to finally read pp198-203 in Buckland et al. 2001 for more insights. My copy should be arriving next week! 

Thank you all for your attention and kindness, 
jeff
